This term means 'to kill' or 'to cause to die'. It carries connotations of destruction and devastation, and in the context of this verse, it emphasizes the extent of the defeat inflicted on the Assyrians. The root of this word also evokes the idea of rendering something lifeless, which in this case illustrates God's power over enemy forces. Theologically, this demonstrates that God is sovereign and capable of acting powerfully to protect His people.

This word means 'camp' or 'army'. It refers to a place where soldiers gather, and in this context, it designates the camp of the Assyrians. The semantic field of this word includes notions of war and conflict, which underscores the threat posed by the Assyrian army to the people of Israel. Spiritually, this reminds us that even in the face of overwhelming adversities, God is capable of intervening decisively.

35.epoque: This passage takes place in the 8th century B.C., during the period of the monarchy of Israel, when the kingdom was threatened by the Assyrian Empire, known for its brutality and conquests.
35.passage: This verse is found in the context of King Hezekiah's prayer, who implores God to save Jerusalem from the Assyrian attack. Chapter 19 recounts how God responds to Hezekiah's supplication by intervening miraculously.
35.culture: In the culture of the time, war was often seen as a struggle between the gods of nations. The defeat of the Assyrians is therefore not only a military victory but also a demonstration of the supremacy of the God of Israel over false gods.
35.interpretation: This verse illustrates God's power that supernaturally protects His people. The divine intervention by the angel shows that even in desperate situations, God is capable of acting to deliver those who trust Him. It also emphasizes the necessity of prayer and faith in times of crisis.
35.commentaire: This account reminds us that God is sovereign and hears the prayers of His people. In our own struggles, we can be assured that God is capable of intervening powerfully and unexpectedly. This verse encourages us to place our trust in God, even when circumstances seem desperate, for He is always at work for our good.

mots.sens: Proper noun referring to the king of Assyria, Sancherib, who led military campaigns against the kingdom of Judah. This name is derived from roots that evoke strength and power, highlighting the formidable nature of this adversary. Spiritually, Sancherib represents the forces that oppose God's will and His people, illustrating the struggle between good and evil.

This verb means 'to encamp' or 'to settle'. It evokes the idea of movement and change of location, often associated with strategic decisions in times of war. In this context, it underscores Sancherib's defeat, who, despite his apparent power, must retreat in the face of divine intervention, reminding believers that God is sovereign over all nations.

Nineveh is the capital of Assyria, a symbol of the power and depravity of that nation. This name is associated with the idea of divine judgment, as Nineveh was also the object of God's mercy during Jonah's preaching. Spiritually, the return to Nineveh can represent a return to the origin of the opposition against God's people, highlighting the continuity of the spiritual struggle.

36.epoque: This passage takes place in the 8th century B.C., during the period when Assyria was a dominant power in the Near East, threatening neighboring kingdoms, including Judah.
36.passage: In this chapter, King Hezekiah of Judah faces the threat of Sancherib, who has besieged Jerusalem. This verse marks a turning point, where Sancherib retreats after receiving a divine response, illustrating God's protection over His people.
36.culture: At this time, military conflicts were frequent, and the conquest of a city was often seen as a demonstration of one god's superiority over another. The defeat of Sancherib is thus a powerful testimony to the sovereignty of Yahweh.
36.interpretation: This verse illustrates God's power in the face of human threats. Sancherib's retreat is a reminder that even when circumstances seem desperate, God is capable of intervening and protecting those who trust Him. It teaches us that our faith should rest on divine sovereignty rather than appearances.
36.commentaire: This passage reminds us that earthly powers, no matter how formidable, cannot compete with God's power. In our own struggles, we must remember that God is our refuge and strength, and that He is always at work to defend His people. As believers, we are called to trust in God, even when challenges seem insurmountable.

mots.sens: Nisroc is an Assyrian god, often associated with hunting. The name may derive from a root meaning 'to fly' or 'to rise,' which could symbolize spiritual elevation or power. In this verse, the mention of Nisroc highlights the idolatry and devotion of a king who turns away from the God of Israel, illustrating the tragedy of human dependence on idols.

Adrammélec is a name that could mean 'servant of the king' or 'noble of royalty.' This character represents rebellion and violence, being one of the sons who murders his father. His act underscores the struggle for power and the tragic consequences of idolatry, where even family can become an instrument of divine judgment.

Ararat is a mountainous region, often associated with the land where Noah's ark came to rest. In this context, fleeing to Ararat may symbolize an attempt to escape divine justice. It also evokes the idea of refuge, but here, it is a flight from the consequences of their actions, emphasizing that rebellion against God leads to destruction.

37.epoque: This passage is set in the context of Assyria in the 8th century B.C., a period marked by military conquests and strong idolatry among the surrounding nations.
37.passage: Chapter 19 of 2 Kings deals with the events surrounding King Hezekiah and the Assyrian threat. This verse concludes the tragic story of Sennacherib, highlighting the fall of idolatry and the sovereignty of God over the kingdoms.
37.culture: In Assyrian culture, idolatry was pervasive, and kings often turned to their gods for strength and protection. The house of Nisroc represents an example of this misplaced devotion.
37.interpretation: This verse illustrates the consequence of idolatry and God's judgment on those who turn away from Him. The death of Sennacherib at the hands of his own sons shows that rebellion against God often leads to internal conflicts and tragedies.
37.commentaire: This passage reminds us that true security is not found in idols or false gods, but in our relationship with the living God. The fall of Sennacherib teaches us that those who oppose God ultimately face divine justice. As believers, we must be careful not to allow things or people to take the place of God in our hearts.
